writing.exampleCaption: Reverse order: the last thing created is the first thing dropped.
writing.explanation:
When a value goes out of scope its Drop implementation runs, and values in a scope drop in reverse declaration order. This is deterministic — no collector decides later — which is what lets Rust manage files, locks, and sockets with the same mechanism it uses for memory.

Rust cleans up owned resources at predictable points. When a scope ends, its local values are dropped in reverse declaration order; nested scopes finish before their outer scope continues. `Drop` is a trait whose `drop` method runs during that cleanup. It can release a file, unlock a mutex guard, or close a connection. Memory is only one resource governed by the same rule.

Follow the `Noisy` example and predict the messages before running it. The inner value is created after the outer values and disappears at the inner closing brace. At the outer closing brace, the remaining locals drop from last declared to first declared. The printed order is evidence of the ownership timeline. Binding a value with a leading underscore still owns it; the underscore only suppresses an unused-variable warning. If you need to release a value earlier, `std::mem::drop(value)` consumes it explicitly.

A destructor should not be where essential business logic hides, because callers cannot see that work from the return type. It should reliably release or finalize a resource. Also remember that moving a value transfers the eventual drop to its new owner; the old binding does not run a second destructor. Try moving one `Noisy` value into a helper function and record where its message appears. The exercise connects scope, movement, and cleanup without relying on a garbage collector or manual free call.

When several fields belong to one struct, their cleanup order follows the struct’s field declaration order after the struct’s own Drop method runs. Keep resource dependencies in mind if one field’s destructor relies on another resource.
